Chapter Three: The Slippery Slope of Justifying Harmful Actions
It usually begins with something small. Maybe it’s a harmless white lie, or bending a rule just a little—something you can easily explain away in the moment. But here’s the thing: once your mind figures out how to justify that first questionable action, the next one feels a little easier. And before you know it, each act of self-justification starts paving the way for bigger mistakes down the road.
Imagine a doctor who makes a misdiagnosis. At first, he feels that sting of guilt, but quickly tells himself the symptoms were confusing, and honestly, anyone could’ve made the same call. But when the patient’s condition gets worse, he starts blaming the patient for not following directions, or maybe the hospital for being short-staffed. The more he justifies, the less likely he is to admit—maybe even to himself—that he made a mistake. Over time, this kind of thinking can create a culture where errors get swept under the rug, lessons aren’t learned, and patients end up paying the price.
And it’s not just about individuals. When entire groups or institutions start spinning their own justifications, the fallout can be huge. Take the criminal justice system. Sometimes, police or prosecutors decide early on that someone’s guilty. Suddenly, every bit of evidence gets twisted to fit that story, while anything that doesn’t match is brushed aside. Even if fresh evidence appears—like a new DNA test or a witness changing their story—it can feel almost impossible to let go of that first decision. The result? Innocent people can wind up behind bars, and the real culprits walk free.
You can see the same pattern in personal relationships, too. Think about a parent who punishes their child a bit too harshly. Later, they might insist it was necessary, that the child really needed to learn a lesson. The more they justify what happened, the harder it gets to admit they might have gone too far. And the child? They may start to believe they deserved it, carrying that feeling with them for years.
What’s truly dangerous here is how reasonable it all feels, one step at a time. Nobody wakes up and decides to become cold or unfair. But our need to see ourselves as good and right can slowly harden us, making us shut out new information or other points of view. Our minds build walls around our past actions, and with each layer, it gets tougher to face the truth.
This isn’t about pointing fingers or blaming people for being imperfect. It’s about recognizing how our natural mental defenses, if we don’t keep an eye on them, can lead us down a path to real harm. The more we understand this process, the better our chances of breaking the cycle—to pause, to reflect, and to really ask ourselves: Are my justifications helping me, or am I just trying to protect my pride?
